title: Why Have We Stopped?
subtitle: Diagnose obstacles and restore useful progress
summary: Stopping well is part of execution. A project needs a meaningful definition of done, feedback about whether the problem was solved, and a conscious decision to continue, change direction, or stop. Momentum is useful only when it remains connected to the goal.

concepts.title: Stopping rule
concepts.body: A stopping rule names evidence that the goal is met, no longer worthwhile, or needs a different approach. When movement stops, diagnose the obstacle before pushing harder. The team may lack a decision, a skill, shared understanding, or confidence that the destination is still useful. Different obstacles need different interventions; more status meetings do not solve all of them.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: The team stops when adoption evidence misses the agreed goal twice.

concepts.title: Feedback
concepts.body: Feedback compares the result with the intended outcome and supplies information for the next decision. Talk with the people doing the work and compare their accounts with the plan. A quiet dependency or unresolved disagreement may be invisible in a progress chart. Surface uncomfortable information early enough that it can still change the route.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Support tickets and usage data provide feedback on whether the rewrite helped.

concepts.title: Momentum
concepts.body: Momentum is useful movement toward a goal; activity without a goal can preserve a failing project. Busy people and many completed tasks can coexist with a stalled outcome. Make the next concrete step and its owner visible. If the original goal no longer makes sense, renegotiate it instead of using activity to avoid that conversation.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A milestone is removed because it no longer serves the regulatory outcome.

concepts.title: Finishing
concepts.body: Finishing includes rollout, follow-through, documentation, and checking that the problem was actually addressed. The last part of a project often contains unglamorous coordination: adoption, cleanup, communication, and operational handoff. Keep ownership clear through that work. A system that is technically ready but nobody can confidently operate has not reached the destination.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: The final handoff includes documentation, ownership, and a post-launch check.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Decide whether to stop
scenario.context: A dashboard rewrite has missed its adoption goal twice. The team has built useful components, but continuing would delay a regulatory fix.

options.label: Stop and salvage
options.benefit: Clarifies the decision and creates a workable path through the stated constraint.
options.cost: Stopping requires acknowledging sunk effort and finding a responsible home for partial work.
options.consequence: You compare evidence with the goal, preserve reusable pieces, and redirect capacity to the regulatory outcome.

options.label: Continue for sunk cost
options.benefit: Feels faster or safer in the immediate moment and preserves a familiar habit.
options.cost: Continuing delays a regulatory fix and makes later cancellation more expensive.
options.consequence: The rewrite gains polish while the important fix waits; morale falls when the same gap is rediscovered.

scenario.debrief: Both options respond to a real constraint. The stronger choice makes ownership and consequences visible, then creates a point to learn and adjust.

quiz.question: A project has stopped moving. What helps before demanding more speed?
options: Diagnose the actual obstacle with the people doing the work
Add the same status meeting every day
quiz.explanation: Missing decisions, dependencies, understanding, and changing goals need different responses.

quiz.question: Many tickets close but the desired outcome remains distant. What should the lead inspect?
options: The number of messages in chat
Whether activity still advances the destination
quiz.explanation: Visible busyness can hide a stalled goal or unresolved dependency.

quiz.question: Who should own the operational handoff at the end of a project?
options: Explicit owners agreed before the handoff
quiz.explanation: Finishing includes operational readiness and follow-through, not only implementation.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.
